Adult Mi-iuy croaker (Miichthys miiuy) are known to reach a maximum recorded total length of 73.8 centimeters, a value that classifies them among the larger sciaenids in the northern South China Sea. Field surveys have documented individuals attaining this size (73.8 centimeters) [Li = 73.8 centimeters], though most commercially landed fish are considerably smaller. In contrast, the total length at which gonadal activity commences is substantially less, with males and females first exhibiting signs of reproductive development at approximately 35 centimeters from the snout to the tip of the caudal fin. This length at puberty (35 centimeters) [Lp = 35 centimeters] marks a critical transition in the species' life history, as it signals the shift from a somatic growth-dominated phase to one that includes reproductive investment. The ecological implication of this relatively late onset of maturity is that immature individuals constitute a significant portion of the population for several years, making the species particularly vulnerable to size-selective fishing pressure before they have had an opportunity to spawn.

Body size at the onset of reproductive life provides a robust foundation for estimating weight-based metrics, given the well-established length-weight relationships for this species. Using the morphometric conversion factor of 0.00851 applied to the total length at puberty cubed, the corresponding estimated wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 451.6 grams. This predicted body mass at the point of first gonadal maturation (451.6 grams) [Wwp = 451.6 grams] represents a considerable energetic investment in somatic tissue prior to any allocation toward gamete production. Comparatively, the ultimate adult wet weight derived from the same morphometric conversion using the maximum recorded total length of 73.8 cm is an order of magnitude larger. Empirical growth models yield an asymptotic body mass of approximately 4,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 4,400 grams] for these maximal dimensions, with the ultimate wet weight reflecting the upper boundary of physiological capacity for this species under typical environmental conditions in its subtropical range.

For Miichthys miiuy, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was measured at 40% [GSI = 40%] when individuals are acclimated to a water temperature of 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C]. The index provides a useful comparative metric for assessing how environmental temperature fluctuations might influence future reproductive investment under shifting climatic regimes.

The early life stages of this croaker are characterized by a rapid developmental pace, a necessity for survival in the plankton-rich yet predator-dense pelagic environment. Incubation of the fertilized eggs under controlled laboratory conditions at 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C] results in hatching after approximately 4 days. This age at birth (approximately 4 days) [ab = approximately 4 days] is remarkably brief, a typical feature of teleost species with small pelagic eggs that rely on warm temperatures to accelerate embryonic development at a temperature of 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C]. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva emerges as a tiny, transparent organism. The wet weight at this initial stage of independence from the egg capsule is extremely low; for a member of the closely related genus Argyrosomus regius, the comparable mass at hatching is on the order of 0.00037 grams, providing a reasonable proxy for the initial mass of Miichthys miiuy larvae, despite the taxonomic distinction. This wet weight at birth value (0.00037 grams) [Wwb = 0.00037 grams] underscores the profound ontogenetic challenge faced by the larva, which must transition to exogenous feeding within a few days.

Longevity in wild populations is often constrained by predation, disease, and fishing mortality, but physiological potential places an upper limit on lifespan that is seldom attained in nature. For Miichthys miiuy, the maximum recorded lifespan has been estimated at approximately 5,475 days, based on otolith increment analysis from individuals collected in regions where water temperatures average 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C]. This life span (5,475 days) [am = 5,475 days] translates to roughly 15 years, a duration that is relatively extended for a sciaenid of this body size, exceeding the typical 8–10 year longevity reported for similarly sized members of the family Sciaenidae inhabiting temperate waters at a temperature of 21.9 °C [T = 21.9 °C]. The observed relationship between temperature and longevity is consistent with the metabolic theory of ecology, wherein the rate of physiological aging is closely tied to ambient thermal conditions. This remarkable longevity means that mature individuals can potentially participate in multiple spawning seasons over their lifetime, contributing to population resilience. The protracted adult phase permits repeated breeding events across a long adult phase, a life-history strategy that offsets the exceptionally high mortality experienced during the vulnerable larval and early juvenile stages and distinguishes this species from shorter-lived sciaenids that rely on a single, high-fecundity spawning event.
